name: Frame frauding

card.summary: Using clothing cut, layering, posture and camera angles to make the shoulders and torso read broader than they are, so the body looks bigger in person and in photos.
card.note: Appearance effects depend on fit, context and camera; the idea is discussed mostly in forums, with tailoring history as background.

quick.overview:
Frame frauding is looksmaxxing slang for making a narrow frame look wider without changing the skeleton. The tools are ordinary: structured jackets and padded shoulders, layering, shirt fit, posture and the angle or lens used for photos.

The payoff is a bigger-looking upper body, usually the shoulder-to-waist silhouette that tailoring has aimed at for a century. Shoulder pads, for example, were designed to widen and square the shoulder line, and fashion history shows the effect has been used on purpose since the early 1900s.
quick.how: Forum guides recommend garments with structure at the shoulder, layering such as overshirts and jackets, trousers and tops that keep the waist looking narrower than the shoulders, and standing posture that opens the chest. Related guides cover 'picture frauding' with angles and lighting and, separately, 'height frauding' with thick-soled shoes and insoles.
quick.risks: No health risks come from clothing choices themselves. Exaggerated padding can look obvious if it does not fit the wearer, and forum members themselves caution against overdoing concealment-type tricks. The effect is for visual impression only and does not change the underlying frame.

lead: Frame frauding is a looksmaxxing term for using clothing, posture and angles to look broader through the shoulders and torso than one's actual skeletal frame. 'Fraud' in this slang means a cosmetic or presentation technique rather than anything dishonest in a legal sense, and forum members apply it to several areas: skin, eyes, height and body frame [1][2].

It helps looks directly by changing perceived silhouette. Tailoring has long done this: shoulder pads were created to make shoulders look broader and less sloped, entered non-athletic menswear in the 1910s, and returned in several fashion cycles [3]. Frame frauding guides on looksmax.org apply the same principle to everyday outfits and to photographs [4][5].
Research specific to frame frauding does not exist; the nearest published material is fashion history on shoulder construction.

chain: Structured shoulders, layering and fit add visual width
Narrower waist relative to shoulders (inverted triangle)
Broader-looking frame in person and in photos
angle.text: Clothing with shoulder structure and fitted waists widens the visual shoulder line, an effect tailors have used for over a century [3]. Posture and camera angle extend the effect in photos [5].

infobox: Shoulder structure, layering, fit, posture, angles

paras: On looksmax.org the word 'frauding' covers any technique that improves apparent looks without changing the underlying feature. An extensive guide in the forum applies it to skin (concealer, tinted sunscreen, blur primer) and to the eye area (darker lash line and kohl to make the sclera appear whiter), and a replier notes that lifts and swelling tricks could also be listed [1]. A separate guide covers height: thick-soled boots with a 1.5 to 2 inch insole as a daily option and an active-wear shoe with a 1 inch insole for a lesser load-out [2].
Dedicated threads exist for frame frauding and for picture frauding, the latter about camera angles and presentation in photographs [4][5].

Fashion history documents the same goal. Padding sewn into garments makes shoulders look broader and less sloped. Shoulder pads originated in American football in 1877, reached non-athletic menswear by the 1910s, were promoted in womenswear by Elsa Schiaparelli from 1931, and returned for the 1980s power-dressing era after Yves Saint Laurent's 1978 collection [3]. Standard men's suits through most of the twentieth century used modest padding to square the shoulder neatly [3]. The result is an inverted-triangle silhouette when paired with a smaller waist [3].

Frauding is treated as a softmaxx: reversible and inexpensive compared with surgery. Guide authors note that the most noticeable features should not be exaggerated, saying over-application of cosmetic products looks obvious [1]. Replies to the height guide debate how convincing such methods look in social settings such as clubs [2].

timeline.event: Shoulder pad invented for American football [3]
Schiaparelli and Rochas introduce padded women's shoulders [3]
Yves Saint Laurent collection begins the 1980s big-shoulder era [3]

lore.intro: Members of looksmax.org present frauding as a low-cost way to bridge a gap between actual and desired features [1][2].

claims.claim: Clothing and posture can make a narrow frame look broader.
claims.believers: Guide authors recommend structured outfits and posture and share before-and-after photos [4][5].
claims.experts: Fashion history documents shoulder padding as a tailoring tool intended to widen the shoulder line [3]. No controlled study of forum techniques has been published.

claims.claim: Camera angle and presentation change how a frame reads in pictures.
claims.believers: A picture frauding thread collects angle and lighting techniques [5].
claims.experts: No published study has examined this specific claim.
